concepts.title: Classes, Objects, and Encapsulation
concepts.description: A class is a blueprint bundling state (fields) and behavior (methods); objects are the individual instances built from it via constructors -- and encapsulation, keeping fields private and exposing behavior deliberately, is what turns a class from a loose bag of data into a type whose invariants you can actually trust.
learningObjectives: Define a class with instance fields, one or more constructors, and instance methods, and explain precisely what new does when an object is created.
Explain what this refers to inside a constructor or instance method, and when it's required to disambiguate a field from a same-named parameter.
Use constructor overloading and constructor chaining with this(...) to avoid duplicating initialization logic across constructors.
Explain why fields are conventionally declared private and exposed only through deliberately-written methods, in terms of invariants the class can guarantee.
Explain why returning a direct reference to a mutable field (like a list or array) from a getter breaks encapsulation even though the field itself is private.
Predict an object's field values after a sequence of constructor calls and mutating method calls.

sections.heading: Classes as Blueprints, Objects as Instances
Constructors: Controlling How an Object Comes Into Existence
Encapsulation: Why Fields Are private and Access Is Deliberate
sections.body:
**Encapsulation** means bundling an object's state together with the code that's allowed to touch it, and deliberately restricting outside access to that state so it can only be read or changed through methods the class itself provides. The conventional Java idiom is: fields are `private`, and any access from outside the class goes through public methods -- getters to read, setters (or more specific, purpose-built methods) to write.

The 'why' here is not stylistic preference -- it's about what a class can actually *guarantee*. A `private double balance` with no public setter, only a `deposit(double amount)` method that rejects negative amounts, can genuinely promise that `balance` never goes negative through any code outside the class -- every path that could change it is one the class itself controls and can validate. A `public double balance` field offers no such guarantee at all: any code anywhere that has a reference to the object can write `account.balance = -500;` directly, bypassing every rule the class might have wanted to enforce, because there's no method in the way to enforce anything. Encapsulation is what makes an object's invariants (rules that should always hold true about its state) something the class can actually defend, rather than something it merely hopes callers will respect.

There's a second, quieter benefit: encapsulation is what lets you *change* a class's internal representation later without breaking code that uses it. If `balance` is private and only ever read through `getBalance()`, you're free to later change how the balance is actually stored internally (split into cents as an `int` to avoid floating-point rounding issues, say) without touching a single line of calling code, as long as `getBalance()` still returns a `double` matching the old contract. A public field offers no such seam -- every caller directly depends on the field's exact type and name, and changing either is now a breaking change everywhere it's used.

sections.heading: The Leaky Getter Trap: private Doesn't Automatically Mean Safe

examples.title: Two Independent Objects From One Class
examples.explanation: `new Counter(0)` and `new Counter(100)` each allocate a fresh object on the heap with their own, independent `count` field -- there is no shared storage between `a` and `b` at all, even though they were built from identical code. Calling `a.increment()` twice mutates only `a`'s own `count`, taking it from 0 to 2; it has zero effect on `b`'s count, which starts from a completely different value (100) and is only ever incremented by the one call `b.increment()` makes directly on it, landing at 101. This is the direct, concrete meaning of 'instance fields' -- each object gets its own copy, and methods called on one object only ever operate on that object's own fields, never another object's, unless the code explicitly passes a reference to that other object in.

examples.title: Constructor Chaining Avoids Duplicated Validation Logic
examples.explanation: The one-argument constructor doesn't repeat the validation or the field assignments at all -- `this(side, side)` delegates straight to the two-argument constructor, passing `side` for both width and height, and that constructor's validation and assignment logic runs exactly as it would for any other caller. Because `this(...)` must be the first statement in a constructor, there's no way to accidentally skip past the validation on this path; every route to constructing a `Rectangle`, however many convenience constructors are added later, funnels through that single two-argument constructor's checks. Calling `new Rectangle(-2.0)` proves this: even though the caller only ever touched the *one*-argument constructor, the exception thrown by the validation inside the two-argument constructor still fires, because chaining is a real method call to that constructor, not a copy-paste of its code.

examples.title: Fixing a Leaky Getter With a Defensive Copy
examples.explanation: `getMembers()` now returns `new ArrayList<>(members)` -- a brand-new list object populated with the same elements, not the original `members` list itself. Calling `snapshot.add("Zoe")` mutates that new, independent list; it has no path back to the actual `members` field living inside `team`, so the real team's roster is completely unaffected. The only sanctioned way to actually change `team`'s roster is `addMember(...)`, which is exactly the point -- the class gets to decide what 'adding a member' means (validation, deduplication, logging, whatever it needs) because there's now no other way in. This is a small, mechanical fix, but it's the difference between a class that merely looks encapsulated (private field, no setter) and one that actually is.

misconceptions.description: Declaring a field private is sufficient, on its own, to fully protect an object's internal state from outside mutation.
misconceptions.clarification: private stops outside code from accessing the field *by name* directly (`obj.field`), but it does nothing to protect the actual object that field refers to, if that object is mutable and a method hands out a direct reference to it. A getter that does `return someMutableField;` gives the caller a live, working reference to the exact same object -- callers can then call mutating methods on it (`.add()`, `.set()`, `.clear()`) and change the class's internal state with the class never knowing. Genuine protection for a mutable field requires either returning a defensive copy from the getter, or exposing only an immutable/read-only view of it -- private alone only closes the direct-field-access door, not the door opened by returning a reference to something mutable.

misconceptions.description: Every class automatically gets a no-argument constructor from Java, regardless of what other constructors you've written.
misconceptions.clarification: Java only supplies the automatic, do-nothing default constructor when a class defines *no* constructors of its own at all. The instant you write even one constructor -- with any parameter list -- that automatic default disappears completely; if you still want callers to be able to write `new MyClass()` with no arguments, you must write that zero-argument constructor yourself, explicitly. This is a common source of a specific compile error (something like `constructor MyClass in class MyClass cannot be applied to given types`) for someone who added a parameterized constructor and then, elsewhere in the code, tried to call the no-argument form they assumed would still be there.

exercises.prompt: What does this program print, and why?
hints: Wallet is a class, so a and b are reference variables. What does `Wallet b = a;` actually copy -- the object, or the reference to it?
Since b and a end up pointing at the same object, does calling deposit through b affect what a sees when it reads balance afterward?
c is created independently with `new Wallet(50.0)` -- it has never had any connection to a or b at all.
exercises.expectedAnswer: 75.0, then 75.0. a and b refer to the same Wallet object, so b.deposit(25.0) is visible through a too, giving 75.0. c is a completely separate object that also had 25.0 deposited into it directly, independently arriving at 75.0 as well -- but for an unrelated reason.
exercises.solutionExplanation: `Wallet b = a;` copies the reference stored in `a` into `b` -- exactly like the array-aliasing behavior from earlier in the course, this does not create a second Wallet object; a and b are now two names for the one and only object created by `new Wallet(50.0)`. Calling `b.deposit(25.0)` mutates that single shared object's balance field from 50.0 to 75.0, and since a points at that same object, `a.getBalance()` correctly reports 75.0 too. `c`, by contrast, is a genuinely separate object created by its own `new Wallet(50.0)` call, with its own independent balance field; depositing 25.0 into it directly also brings it to 75.0, but this is a coincidence of using the same numbers, not any shared state -- c was never aliased to a or b at any point.

exercises.prompt: This class is meant to guarantee that an Employee's salary is never set to a negative number, but the bug below shows that guarantee doesn't actually hold. Find and fix the bug.
hints: The constructor's validation only runs once, when the object is first created. Is there any OTHER way, besides the constructor, that code outside the class can change salary?
Look at how salary is declared -- is it actually private, the way name is?
Making the field private removes the direct-assignment path entirely; you'll then need a method (a setter) that re-runs the same validation for any later changes.
exercises.solutionExplanation: The constructor's validation only ever runs at construction time -- it says nothing about what happens afterward, and `salary` was declared `public`, which means any code anywhere with a reference to an Employee could write `e.salary = -1000.0;` directly, completely bypassing the constructor and its check. The fix has two parts: make `salary` `private`, which removes the direct-assignment path entirely (that line would now fail to compile from outside the class), and add a `setSalary` method that re-runs the same validation before actually changing the field, giving the class a controlled, single path for changing salary after construction. This is exactly the earlier lesson about private not being automatic protection taken to its logical conclusion: the constructor validating on the way in is worthless if a public field lets anyone walk around it on the way out.

assessments.prompt: A class has a private field `private List<String> items;` and a getter `public List<String> getItems() { return items; }`. What is the problem with this getter, if any?
options: There is no problem -- private fields are always fully protected regardless of what a getter returns.

The getter returns a direct reference to the actual internal list, so any caller can mutate the class's internal state (via .add(), .remove(), etc.) without going through any method the class controls.
This code fails to compile, because a getter cannot return a reference type.
The problem is that getItems() should be named differently, since 'get' should only be used for primitive fields.
assessments.explanation: Returning `items` directly hands the caller the exact same List object the class holds internally -- since lists are mutable, the caller can call mutating methods on that reference and change the class's actual internal state, with the class having no say in it and no way to validate the change. Option A is the misconception this concept specifically warns against: private only blocks direct field access by name, not mutation through a returned reference to a mutable object. Option C is wrong -- returning a reference type from a getter is completely ordinary and legal. Option D is a fabricated, irrelevant naming rule; the actual problem is structural, not cosmetic.

assessments.prompt: Explain what encapsulation actually buys a class, using the idea of invariants, and explain why a private field with a getter that leaks a mutable reference only provides the appearance of encapsulation rather than the real thing.
assessments.modelAnswer: Encapsulation means bundling an object's state with the code permitted to touch it, and routing every outside interaction with that state through methods the class itself writes and controls -- typically by making fields private and exposing only deliberately-chosen public methods. The payoff is that the class can actually guarantee its invariants: rules about its own state that should always hold true, like a bank balance never going negative or a list never containing duplicate entries. If every path that can change that state is a method the class wrote, the class can put a check at the top of that method and be certain -- not hopeful, certain -- that the check is enforced on every single call, because there is no other way in. A public field offers no such guarantee: any code anywhere holding a reference to the object can assign directly to that field, bypassing every rule the class might want to enforce, since there's no method standing in the way to enforce anything. The subtler failure mode is a field that's private, with no public setter, but a getter that returns the actual internal object when that object happens to be mutable -- an ArrayList, say, rather than an int. This looks encapsulated from the outside: there's no way to write `obj.field = ...` directly. But the caller who receives that returned list can call .add() or .remove() or .clear() on it, and because it's the exact same object the class holds internally -- not a copy -- those mutations land directly on the class's real internal state, with the class having no idea it happened and no chance to validate or reject it. The fix is a defensive copy: return a new collection built from the internal one, so callers can look at (or even freely mutate their own copy of) the data without any of it reaching back into the object's actual internals. Real encapsulation requires thinking about every path data can flow out through, not just whether the field keyword happens to say private.

assessments.prompt: class Point { private int x; private int y; public Point(int x, int y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; } } Point p = new Point(); What happens?
options: This compiles fine, since Java always provides a no-argument constructor for every class, regardless of what else is declared.

This fails to compile, because the moment a class defines any constructor of its own, the automatic no-argument default constructor disappears entirely -- Point has no accessible zero-argument constructor for new Point() to call.
This compiles fine and creates a Point with x and y both defaulting to 0.
This throws a NullPointerException at run time, since x and y are never initialized.
assessments.explanation: Java only supplies the automatic, do-nothing default constructor when a class defines no constructors at all. Point defines one constructor, taking (int, int), so that automatic default is gone -- there is no zero-argument constructor available for new Point() to invoke, and the compiler rejects the call rather than inventing one. Option A describes behavior that only holds for classes with no constructors written at all. Option C assumes a default constructor exists when it does not. Option D is wrong because this code never reaches run time in the first place -- the failure is caught by javac before any object could ever be created.

assessments.prompt: class Person { private String name; public Person(String name) { name = name; } public String getName() { return name; } } What does new Person("Amy").getName() return, and why?
options: "Amy", because name = name correctly assigns the constructor parameter's value into the field.

null, because the bare name on the left of name = name refers to the parameter, which shadows the field inside the constructor -- the assignment sets the parameter to itself, and the field name never receives the argument at all, keeping its default value.
This fails to compile, because Java forbids assigning a variable to itself.
"", because uninitialized String fields default to an empty string rather than null.
assessments.explanation: Inside the constructor, the parameter name shadows the field of the same name -- a bare name refers to the parameter, not this.name, unless this. is written explicitly. name = name is therefore a self-assignment of the parameter to itself; it never touches the field. Since String fields default to null when never explicitly assigned, getName() returns null, not "Amy". This is exactly the reflexive-this.field-name bug the material warns about: it compiles without any error and produces no exception, just a silently wrong result. Option A assumes the bare name resolves to the field, which is precisely the shadowing mistake. Option C is wrong because self-assignment is completely legal Java. Option D is wrong about String's actual default value, which is null, not an empty string.

assessments.prompt: public class Rectangle { private double width, height; public Rectangle(double width, double height) { if (width <= 0 || height <= 0) { throw new IllegalArgumentException("invalid"); } this.width = width; this.height = height; } public Rectangle(double side) { System.out.println("creating square"); this(side, side); } } What is wrong with the second constructor?
options: Nothing -- this compiles and works exactly as intended.
This fails to compile, because a call to this(...) must be the very first statement in a constructor, and here it's preceded by a println statement.
This fails to compile, because a constructor is never allowed to call another constructor of the same class under any circumstance.
This compiles fine but silently skips the validation logic in the two-argument constructor.
assessments.explanation: Constructor chaining via this(...) is required to be the first statement in the constructor body -- Java enforces this so that an object's initialization always resolves down to one real path of field assignments, with nothing able to run before that delegation happens. Placing the println before this(side, side) violates that rule directly, so this fails to compile. Option A is wrong because this specific ordering is a real, enforced restriction. Option C is wrong because this(...) chaining is exactly what the surrounding material demonstrates working correctly, provided it's the first statement. Option D describes a plausible-sounding but incorrect outcome -- if it compiled, chaining would still run the validation; the actual problem is that it does not compile at all.

concepts.title: Inheritance: extends and super
concepts.description: Inheritance lets one class (a subclass) acquire the fields and methods of another (a superclass) via extends, and override specific methods to specialize behavior; super is how a subclass explicitly reaches back to its superclass's constructor or an overridden method -- and understanding exactly when each runs is what separates confident subclassing from cargo-culted syntax.
learningObjectives: Define a subclass with extends and explain what it inherits automatically from its superclass, and what it does not (private members, constructors).
Override an inherited method correctly using @Override, and explain how the actual (run-time) type of an object -- not the declared type of the reference -- determines which overridden version runs.
Explain why a subclass constructor must invoke a superclass constructor, implicitly or explicitly via super(...), as its very first action.
Use super.methodName() to call an overridden superclass method from inside the overriding subclass method, and explain when this is necessary.
Distinguish overriding from overloading, and predict compile errors caused by an invalid @Override.
Trace the exact order of constructor calls up an inheritance chain when a subclass object is created.

sections.heading: extends: What a Subclass Actually Inherits
Constructors Aren't Inherited -- super(...) Chains Them Instead
Overriding: Same Signature, New Body, Chosen at Run Time
super.method(): Reaching Back to the Overridden Version

examples.title: Constructor Chaining Order Up an Inheritance Hierarchy
examples.explanation: Even though none of these constructors writes an explicit `super()` call, Java silently inserts `super()` as the first statement of every constructor that doesn't call one explicitly -- so `Puppy()`'s implicit first action is calling `Dog()`'s constructor, whose own implicit first action is calling `Animal()`'s constructor, whose implicit first action calls `Object`'s (built-in, does nothing observable here). Execution therefore runs top-down from the top of the hierarchy: `Animal`'s body finishes first (printing 'Animal constructor'), then control returns to `Dog`'s body, which finishes next ('Dog constructor'), and only then does `Puppy`'s own body finally run ('Puppy constructor'). This ordering is not incidental -- it guarantees that by the time any subclass constructor body starts executing its own logic, every superclass's fields have already been fully initialized by that superclass's own constructor.

examples.title: Overriding Is Resolved by Run-Time Type, Not Declared Type
examples.explanation: Every element of the `shapes` array is *declared* as `Shape`, but each one's *actual* object is a `Circle` or a `Square`, and `s.area()` dispatches based on that actual, run-time type every single time through the loop -- the exact same line of code, `s.area()`, runs a completely different method body depending on which real object `s` currently refers to. This is the entire practical payoff of overriding: code written once, against the general `Shape` type, correctly runs each specific subclass's own specialized behavior without needing an if/else or switch checking 'is this a Circle or a Square' anywhere. `Shape` itself never needs to know how many kinds of shapes will eventually exist -- any new subclass that overrides `area()` correctly would work in this same loop with zero changes to the loop itself.

examples.title: super.method() Extends Behavior Instead of Duplicating It
examples.explanation: `Manager.calculatePay()` doesn't reimplement the base salary logic at all -- `super.calculatePay()` calls Employee's own version explicitly, which returns `baseSalary` (80000.0), and Manager's override simply adds `bonus` (15000.0) on top of that, giving 95000.0. If Employee's pay calculation later grew more complex (say, factoring in years of service), Manager's override would automatically pick up that change through `super.calculatePay()`, with zero edits needed in Manager itself. Contrast this with what would happen if Manager's override called `this.calculatePay()` instead of `super.calculatePay()`: since `this` always dispatches to the real run-time type's version, and the real run-time type here is Manager, `this.calculatePay()` would call Manager's own override again, which would call itself again, and so on -- an infinite recursion ending in a StackOverflowError, not the intended behavior at all.

misconceptions.description: A subclass automatically inherits its superclass's constructors, the same way it inherits methods.
misconceptions.clarification: Constructors are specifically excluded from what extends hands down. A subclass must define its own constructors, and every one of them must invoke some constructor of the superclass -- implicitly (an inserted, no-argument super()) or explicitly (a super(...) call you write yourself) -- as its first action. This isn't a minor exception; it's a core structural rule: superclass state has to be properly initialized by the superclass's own constructor logic before subclass initialization can safely begin, and that can only happen if every subclass constructor genuinely triggers it.

misconceptions.description: Calling an overridden method through a variable declared as the superclass type runs the superclass's version of that method, since that's the declared type.
misconceptions.clarification: Overriding is resolved by the object's actual, run-time type, completely independent of how the reference variable holding it happens to be declared. `Animal a = new Dog();` followed by `a.makeSound();` runs Dog's overriding version, not Animal's -- the declared type `Animal` only constrains which methods and fields you're allowed to reference through `a` at compile time (you couldn't call a Dog-only method through an Animal-typed reference without a cast), it does not determine which overridden method body actually executes. That dispatch decision is made at run time, based on the real object, which is exactly why this mechanism is called run-time polymorphism.

exercises.prompt: What does this print, and why?
hints: Constructing a Car always runs Vehicle's constructor first, whether or not super() is written explicitly -- track the print order across both constructors.
v is declared as Vehicle, but the actual object is a Car -- which describe() actually runs when v.describe() is called?
Inside Car's describe(), super.describe() calls Vehicle's own version specifically, not Car's -- trace what string that produces and how Car's override builds on top of it.
exercises.expectedAnswer:
Vehicle created
Car created
a car, which is a vehicle. Construction prints top-down (superclass first), and describe() dispatches to Car's override based on the real run-time type, which itself calls super.describe() to build on Vehicle's text.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Constructing `new Car()` first runs Vehicle's constructor (via the explicit super() call, which must be the first statement), printing 'Vehicle created', and only then does Car's own constructor body run, printing 'Car created'. After construction, v.describe() is called through a reference declared as Vehicle, but the actual object is a Car, and overriding dispatches based on that real type -- so Car's override runs. Inside it, super.describe() explicitly calls Vehicle's version, returning 'a vehicle', and Car's override appends that into 'a car, which is a vehicle', which is what ultimately gets printed.

exercises.prompt: This code is meant to have Square override Rectangle's area() calculation, but it fails to compile. Find and fix the bug.
hints: Every subclass constructor's first action must be a call to some superclass constructor -- is Square's constructor doing that anywhere, explicitly or implicitly?
Rectangle has no accessible no-argument constructor at all, so Java can't silently insert one for Square -- what does that mean for Square's constructor?
Separately, check the method name Square is trying to override very carefully against Rectangle's actual method name -- Java method names are case-sensitive.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Two separate bugs here. First, Square's constructor tries to assign width and height directly without ever calling a Rectangle constructor -- but every subclass constructor's first statement must be a call to a superclass constructor, and since Rectangle has no accessible no-argument constructor for Java to insert implicitly, this fails to compile with something like 'constructor Rectangle in class Rectangle cannot be applied to given types' or a missing-super error. The fix replaces the direct field assignments with super(side, side), letting Rectangle's own constructor do the actual initialization. Second, the method is written as Area() (capital A), which does not match Rectangle's area() (lowercase a) -- @Override specifically catches this: since there's no Rectangle method with that exact signature to override, the annotation itself makes this a compile error rather than silently letting Area() become an unrelated new method that never actually overrides anything. Renaming it to area() fixes the mismatch and makes @Override valid.

options: A
B, and A
B
This fails to compile because ref is declared as A but assigned a B.
assessments.explanation: ref is declared as A, but its actual, run-time object is a B, and overriding dispatches based on that real type -- so ref.greet() runs B's override, not A's. Inside B's override, super.greet() explicitly calls A's version, which returns "A", and B's override concatenates that into "B, and A", which is exactly what gets printed. Option A wrongly assumes the declared type determines which override runs. Option C ignores that super.greet() contributes to the result. Option D is wrong -- assigning a subclass object to a superclass-typed reference is completely legal and is, in fact, the entire basis of polymorphism.

assessments.prompt: A junior developer is confused about why their subclass constructor won't compile without a super(...) call, when their superclass 'obviously' has fields that need initializing anyway. Explain the rule around subclass constructors and super(...), and separately explain how overriding differs from overloading in terms of when the actual method to run is decided.
assessments.modelAnswer: Every subclass constructor's very first action, whether you write it explicitly or not, must be a call to some constructor of its superclass. If you don't write a super(...) call yourself, Java automatically inserts a call to the superclass's no-argument constructor as the first line -- but that only works if the superclass actually has an accessible no-argument constructor. If the superclass only defines constructors that take arguments, that automatic insertion has nothing valid to call, and the subclass constructor fails to compile unless you write an explicit super(...) call yourself, matching one of the superclass's real constructors. The reason this is enforced so strictly is structural: a subclass typically inherits fields from its superclass, and those fields need to be properly initialized by the superclass's own constructor logic before the subclass constructor's body does anything that might depend on them being in a valid state. Java guarantees this by making superclass construction unconditionally happen first, all the way up the inheritance chain, before any subclass's own constructor body runs its own statements. Separately, overriding and overloading are resolved completely differently, despite sounding similar. Overloading -- multiple methods sharing a name but differing in parameter list -- is resolved entirely at compile time, purely from the declared types of the arguments at each call site; the compiler bakes in which specific overload a given call will invoke before the program ever runs. Overriding -- a subclass redefining an inherited method with the identical signature -- is resolved at run time, based on the actual, real type of the object a method is called on, regardless of how the reference variable pointing at that object happens to be declared. That's why calling a method through a superclass-typed reference that actually points at a subclass object still runs the subclass's overridden version: the decision is deferred to run time and depends on what the object really is, not on the compile-time type of the variable used to reach it.

assessments.prompt: class Animal { private String name; protected int age; public Animal(String name, int age) { this.name = name; this.age = age; } } class Dog extends Animal { public Dog(String name, int age) { super(name, age); } public void printAge() { System.out.println(age); } public void printName() { System.out.println(name); } } What happens when Dog is compiled?
options: Both printAge() and printName() compile fine, since Dog inherits both fields from Animal.

printAge() compiles fine because age is protected, which subclass code can reference directly; printName() fails to compile because name is private in Animal -- every Dog object still carries that field's storage, but Dog's own code cannot refer to it directly by name.
Both methods fail to compile, because a subclass can never directly reference any field declared in a superclass.
printName() compiles fine because private members automatically become protected once a class is inherited by a subclass.
assessments.explanation: protected grants access to subclasses in addition to the declaring class itself, so Dog's code can reference age directly, and printAge() compiles fine. private, by contrast, restricts access to the declaring class only -- Dog still has the storage for name (every Dog object carries it), but Dog's own code has no direct way to name it, exactly the same as any unrelated outside code would face. Option A overlooks that inheriting a field's storage is different from being able to reference it by name. Option C is wrong because protected fields are specifically designed to be accessible from subclasses. Option D is wrong -- access modifiers are fixed at declaration and are never upgraded by the mere fact of being inherited.

assessments.prompt: class Base { public Base(int id) { } } class Derived extends Base { public Derived() { } } What happens when this is compiled?
options: It compiles fine; Java inserts an implicit super() call using a no-argument constructor on Base.

It fails to compile, because Java tries to insert an implicit super() call as Derived's first action, but Base has no accessible no-argument constructor for that call to match -- Derived's constructor must instead explicitly call super(someInt).
It compiles fine, because Derived's constructor body has no statements of its own, so no superclass constructor call is required at all.
It fails to compile because Base's constructor parameter must share the same name as one used somewhere in Derived's constructor.
assessments.explanation: Every subclass constructor's first action, explicit or not, must be a call to some superclass constructor. Derived writes no explicit super(...) call, so Java tries to insert the implicit super() -- but Base only defines a constructor that takes an int, so there's no accessible no-argument constructor for that implicit call to match, and compilation fails. The fix would be writing super(someInt) explicitly as Derived's first statement. Option A assumes a no-argument constructor exists on Base when it does not. Option C is wrong because an empty constructor body still needs a superclass constructor call; 'first action' applies regardless of whether any other statements follow. Option D describes a rule Java has no version of at all -- parameter names never need to match across a super call.

assessments.prompt: class Animal { public void makeSound(String context) { } } class Dog extends Animal { @Override public void makeSound() { } } What happens when Dog is compiled?
options: It compiles fine, and makeSound() overrides Animal's makeSound(String) since they share the same name.

It fails to compile, because @Override asserts this method overrides a superclass method, but Animal has no makeSound method with an empty parameter list -- the differing parameter list makes this a distinct, unrelated method rather than an override, and the annotation catches that mismatch.
It compiles fine, silently defining a new overloaded method alongside Animal's, with @Override simply having no effect.
It fails to compile because a subclass is never allowed to declare a method sharing a name already used in its superclass.
assessments.explanation: Overriding requires an identical signature -- same name AND same parameter types. makeSound() and makeSound(String) differ in parameter list, so Dog's method would ordinarily just be a new, unrelated overload rather than an override of Animal's method. Because @Override explicitly asserts an overriding intent, the compiler checks for a genuinely matching superclass method, finds none with a matching signature, and reports a compile error instead of silently letting the mismatch through. Option A is wrong because differing parameter lists never produce an override, regardless of a shared name. Option C describes exactly what would happen without @Override present -- the annotation's entire purpose is to turn that silent outcome into a caught error. Option D is wrong because declaring a same-named method with a different parameter list (an overload) is completely legal on its own; the actual problem here is specifically the incorrect @Override claim.

concepts.title: Interfaces vs. Abstract Classes
concepts.description: Both interfaces and abstract classes let you declare behavior without fully implementing it, forcing subclasses/implementers to fill in the gaps -- but they solve genuinely different design problems: an abstract class models 'is-a' with shared state and partial implementation, while an interface models 'can-do' capability contracts that unrelated classes can adopt, including through multiple inheritance of type.
learningObjectives: Declare an abstract class with a mix of abstract and concrete methods, and explain why an abstract class cannot be instantiated directly with new.
Declare an interface with abstract methods and implement it in an unrelated class, and explain why a class can implement multiple interfaces but extend only one class.
Explain what a default method on an interface is for, and how it differs from an abstract method on that same interface.
Decide, given a design scenario, whether an abstract class or an interface (or both together) is the right tool, based on whether shared state/implementation or a pure capability contract is needed.
Predict and explain a compile error caused by a concrete subclass failing to implement every abstract method it inherits from an abstract superclass or interface.
Explain what happens when two interfaces both provide a default method with the same signature and a class implements both.

sections.heading: Abstract Classes: Partial Implementation, and a Promise Subclasses Must Keep
Interfaces: A Pure Capability Contract, Implementable by Any Class
default Methods: Interfaces That Can Actually Implement Something
Choosing Between Them, and What Happens When Both Are Combined
sections.body:
The practical rule of thumb: reach for an **abstract class** when subclasses genuinely share state (fields) and you want to write real, shared implementation once, at the top, with only specific pieces deliberately left open for subclasses to specialize -- it models a true 'is-a' hierarchy of closely related types. Reach for an **interface** when you're describing a capability that unrelated classes might adopt independently of any inheritance relationship, especially when a single class plausibly needs several such capabilities at once. In real, non-trivial designs, these aren't mutually exclusive -- it's completely normal for an abstract class to itself implement one or more interfaces, providing shared partial implementation for concrete subclasses while also satisfying a broader capability contract other, unrelated classes satisfy differently.

One edge case worth knowing about explicitly: if a class implements two interfaces that each provide a *default* method with the exact same signature, Java does not pick one arbitrarily and does not silently prefer either -- it's a compile error (something like 'class X inherits unrelated defaults for greet() from types A and B') unless the class itself overrides that method, providing its own implementation (which may, if it chooses, call `InterfaceA.super.greet()` or `InterfaceB.super.greet()` explicitly to pick one, or combine them). This is Java's deliberate, conservative answer to the diamond problem for default methods: rather than guessing at a resolution the way some languages do, it forces the class author to resolve the conflict explicitly, on the theory that a silent, arbitrary choice would be far more dangerous than a compile error demanding a decision.

examples.title: Abstract Class With Shared Implementation and One Abstract Method
examples.explanation: totalPay() is written once, in the abstract Employee class, and it's never duplicated in SalesEmployee -- it calls bonus(), which Employee deliberately leaves abstract, trusting every concrete subclass to supply a real implementation. SalesEmployee only has to implement bonus() (5% of sales, here); it gets totalPay() correctly, for free, and that shared logic would apply identically to any other future Employee subclass (a SalariedManager with a flat bonus, say) without totalPay() itself ever needing to change. Employee could never be instantiated directly -- new Employee("x", 1000.0) would fail to compile -- specifically because bonus() has no body anywhere in Employee itself, and calling e.totalPay() on a genuinely incomplete object would have no real bonus() to call.

examples.title: One Class, Two Independent Interface Contracts
examples.explanation: Order implements two completely independent interfaces at once -- something it could not do with class inheritance, since Java only permits extending one class. Chargeable and Refundable have no relationship to each other at all; they're two separate capability contracts that happen to both make sense for the same Order class to satisfy. Nothing about implementing Chargeable constrains or interferes with implementing Refundable -- each interface only requires one specific method, and Order is free to implement both however it likes, sharing whatever internal state (total, cancelled) it needs between them. Code elsewhere that only cares about the charging side can be written against the Chargeable type alone, with zero awareness that Order also happens to be Refundable.

examples.title: A default Method Provides a Working Fallback
examples.explanation: ConsoleLogger only ever implements log(), the one genuinely abstract method Logger requires. logError() is never written in ConsoleLogger at all -- it's inherited directly from Logger's default implementation, which itself is built entirely out of a call to log(). Because that call dispatches to whatever concrete log() implementation the actual object provides (ConsoleLogger's, here), logError() correctly produces 'ERROR: disk full' printed to the console, even though Logger itself has no idea, and doesn't need to know, that console printing is how log() actually happens. If a different implementer, say FileLogger, wrote its own log() that appended to a file instead, that exact same inherited logError() default would automatically write 'ERROR: ...' to a file instead, with zero changes needed to Logger or to logError() itself.

misconceptions.description: Since both abstract classes and interfaces can declare methods with no body that subclasses must implement, they're basically interchangeable design tools, and the choice between them is mostly a matter of taste.
misconceptions.clarification: They solve structurally different problems, and the choice has real consequences a class only discovers once it's too late to easily change: a class can extend only one abstract class, but it can implement any number of interfaces. An abstract class is the right tool specifically when you want to share real state (fields) and real implementation across closely related subclasses, modeling a genuine 'is-a' hierarchy where only some behavior is deliberately left open. An interface is the right tool for a capability contract that unrelated classes might adopt independently -- especially when a class plausibly needs to satisfy several such contracts simultaneously, which committing to a single abstract-class hierarchy would foreclose. Picking an abstract class when you actually needed a class to also satisfy an unrelated second contract later is a design mistake that can force a significant, breaking restructure -- it is not a cosmetic choice.

misconceptions.description: A default method on an interface lets that interface store and share state across all the classes that implement it, the same way a field on an abstract class does.
misconceptions.clarification: A default method can only provide a shared method BODY -- an implementation that all implementers get for free -- it cannot introduce any instance field at all; interfaces still have no per-object storage of their own. A default method's body can only read from and combine the results of other methods (abstract or default) the interface declares -- it cannot maintain its own persistent state between calls the way a field on an abstract class naturally does, because there is no interface-level storage for it to live in. If shared, per-object mutable state is genuinely required, that's a strong specific signal pointing toward an abstract class (or plain composition) instead of an interface.

exercises.prompt: What does this program print, and why?
hints: EmailNotifier never implements send() or sendUrgent() itself -- trace where each one actually comes from in the chain of interface and abstract class.
sendUrgent() is a default method that calls send(message) -- and that call dispatches to whatever real, run-time implementation of send() the actual object provides, exactly like overriding does.
BaseNotifier's send() uses prefix, which was set via the constructor chain -- figure out what prefix actually holds for this specific EmailNotifier object.
exercises.expectedAnswer: EMAIL: URGENT: server down. sendUrgent (the interface default) calls send("URGENT: server down"), which dispatches to BaseNotifier's implementation, printing prefix ("EMAIL") followed by the message.
exercises.solutionExplanation: n.sendUrgent("server down") runs Notifier's default method, since neither BaseNotifier nor EmailNotifier overrides it. That default builds the string "URGENT: server down" and calls send(...) with it -- and that call dispatches based on the real run-time type of n, which is an EmailNotifier. EmailNotifier itself has no send() of its own, but it inherits BaseNotifier's implementation, which prints prefix + ": " + message. prefix was set to "EMAIL" via EmailNotifier's constructor calling super("EMAIL"), so the final output is "EMAIL: URGENT: server down" -- a chain running from the interface's default, into the abstract class's concrete implementation, using state set up by the concrete subclass's constructor.

exercises.prompt: This code is meant to define a Payable interface implemented by an abstract Worker class, with a concrete Contractor subclass. It fails to compile. Find and fix the bug.
hints: Worker implements Payable but is itself declared abstract -- does an abstract class have to actually implement every method of an interface it declares implements?
Contractor is a concrete (non-abstract) class -- concrete classes CANNOT leave any inherited abstract method (from an interface OR an abstract superclass) unimplemented.
Add a calculatePay() implementation to Contractor, using hourlyRate and hoursWorked to compute the actual pay.
exercises.solutionExplanation: Worker is allowed to implement Payable without providing calculatePay() itself, precisely because Worker is declared abstract -- an abstract class is permitted to leave inherited abstract methods (whether from an interface or from an abstract superclass) unimplemented, deferring the obligation to whichever subclass eventually becomes concrete. Contractor, however, is a plain, concrete class, and a concrete class is never allowed to leave any inherited abstract method unimplemented -- since Contractor extends Worker and never supplies calculatePay(), the compiler correctly rejects it with something like 'Contractor is not abstract and does not override abstract method calculatePay() in Payable'. The fix adds a real calculatePay() implementation to Contractor, computing pay from its own hourlyRate and hoursWorked fields, which finally satisfies the obligation Payable originally imposed and Worker deliberately left open.

assessments.prompt: A class needs to share a considerable amount of common state and implemented logic across several closely related subclasses, AND separately needs to be usable anywhere a totally unrelated 'Comparable'-style capability is expected. Which design is most appropriate?
options: Use only an interface for everything, since interfaces are strictly more flexible than abstract classes.

Use an abstract class as the shared base for the closely related subclasses (for the shared state and implementation), and have that abstract class also implement the unrelated capability interface -- these are not mutually exclusive.
Use only an abstract class for everything, and have the unrelated capability re-implemented separately by each subclass instead of using an interface.
This scenario is impossible to model correctly in Java, since a class cannot both extend a class and implement an interface.
assessments.explanation: Abstract classes and interfaces are not mutually exclusive tools -- a class (including an abstract one) can extend at most one class while implementing any number of interfaces at the same time. Using an abstract class to hold the shared state and implementation for closely related subclasses, while that same abstract class also implements the unrelated capability interface, lets every concrete subclass automatically get both: the shared implementation via inheritance, and the capability contract via the interface it's already implementing. Option A is wrong because interfaces cannot hold shared instance state the way this scenario requires. Option C needlessly duplicates the capability's contract across every subclass instead of declaring it once. Option D is factually wrong -- extending a class and implementing interfaces simultaneously is completely standard and exactly what this scenario calls for.

assessments.prompt: A teammate asks: 'Why does Java let a class implement multiple interfaces but only extend one class -- isn't that an arbitrary, inconsistent restriction?' Explain why it isn't arbitrary, and give the practical rule of thumb for choosing between an abstract class and an interface.
assessments.modelAnswer: It isn't arbitrary -- it's a direct consequence of what each mechanism is allowed to carry. Extending a class inherits real implementation and real instance state: fields with actual values, and method bodies that may depend on that state. If Java allowed a class to extend two classes that each defined, say, a field named total with different meanings, or two conflicting implementations of the same method, there would be a genuine, unresolvable ambiguity about which field or which method body the subclass actually has -- this is the classic 'diamond problem,' and rather than inventing an arbitrary tie-breaking rule the way some languages do, Java avoids the situation entirely by disallowing multiple class inheritance. Interfaces, historically, declared no state and no implementation at all -- purely method signatures, contracts about what a class can do -- so there was never any state or implementation to conflict between two interfaces a class chose to implement; adopting five unrelated capability contracts on one class is perfectly safe because there's nothing shared between them to collide. Java 8's default methods reintroduced a limited form of shared implementation into interfaces, and true to the underlying concern, Java does force an explicit resolution -- a compile error -- in the one case where two implemented interfaces both provide a default method with the same signature, rather than silently picking one. As a practical rule of thumb: reach for an abstract class when you want to share real state and implementation across a family of closely related types, modeling genuine 'is-a' ancestry with only specific behavior deliberately left open; reach for an interface when you're describing a capability that unrelated classes might adopt independently, especially when a single class plausibly needs to satisfy several such capabilities at once -- and remember the two combine freely, since a class extending one abstract class can still implement as many interfaces as it needs.

assessments.prompt: abstract class Shape { public abstract double area(); } Shape s = new Shape(); What happens?
options: This compiles fine, creating a Shape object whose area() acts as an empty stub that does nothing when called.

This fails to compile, because Shape is abstract and Java refuses to let it be instantiated directly with new -- there is a real, structural gap (area() has no body anywhere in Shape) that would leave an incomplete object.
This compiles fine but throws an exception the first time area() is actually called on s.
This fails to compile only because Shape has no constructor defined -- adding one would make new Shape() legal.
assessments.explanation: An abstract class is incomplete by design -- it can declare abstract methods with no body at all, and Java enforces, at compile time, that you can never instantiate such a class directly, precisely because doing so would produce an object with a method that has nowhere to dispatch to. new Shape() is rejected before the program ever runs. Option A and C both assume instantiation is allowed and only differ on when the problem would show up -- but the problem is caught immediately, at compile time, not deferred to construction or to calling area(). Option D is wrong because adding a constructor to Shape would not change its abstractness at all; the restriction comes from the abstract keyword and the unimplemented method, not from the absence of a constructor.

assessments.prompt: interface A { default String greet() { return "A"; } } interface B { default String greet() { return "B"; } } class C implements A, B { } What happens when C is compiled?
options: It compiles fine, and C's greet() returns "A", since interfaces are resolved in the order they're listed in implements.
It fails to compile with an error about inheriting unrelated defaults for greet() from A and B, unless C itself overrides greet() to resolve the conflict explicitly.
It compiles fine, and C's greet() returns "B", since the last interface listed always wins the conflict.
It compiles fine, and calling c.greet() throws a runtime exception because Java cannot decide which version to run.
assessments.explanation: When a class implements two interfaces that each supply a default method with the exact same signature, Java does not pick one arbitrarily by listing order or any other implicit rule -- it treats the conflict as a compile error, forcing the class author to resolve it explicitly by overriding greet() in C (optionally calling A.super.greet() or B.super.greet() to pick one, or combining them). This is a deliberate, conservative design choice: a silent, arbitrary resolution would be more dangerous than demanding the author decide. Options A and C both invent a resolution-by-order rule that Java does not have. Option D is wrong because the failure happens at compile time, not as a runtime exception -- C never successfully compiles in the first place, so it could never be instantiated to call greet() on.
